title: US Readies 'Most Crushing Economic Operation' Against Iran as Tehran Calls Sanctions Support an 'Act of War'
subhead: Washington is shifting the Iran conflict from the battlefield to a coordinated economic-isolation campaign aimed at collapsing the regime, with details due today. Canada walked away from trade talks with the White House, and a new peace roadmap emerged for eastern DR Congo.

sections.heading: Washington Opens an Economic Front Against Iran
sections.body:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC that Washington is preparing to 'squash' the Iranian economy and 'collapse this regime,' warning allies that 'you are either with us or against us.' He said the planned pressure campaign would minimise the need for a 'large-scale kinetic restart' of the conflict, and confirmed further details would be made public at a press conference on 24 August, according to the BBC.

Tehran has pushed back hard. Iran's security chief said support for new US sanctions would be an 'act of war,' per AP. The 60-day memorandum of understanding that President Donald Trump signed in June — setting a deadline for ending the war and reaching a nuclear accord — lapsed last week with the two sides still far apart, notably on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, through which some 20 percent of the world's oil and LNG once transited. President Masoud Pezeshkian has linked the stalled agreement to Iran's inability to attract investment.
sections.whyItMatters: This marks a deliberate pivot from military strikes to economic warfare as the primary lever against Iran, forcing every US ally and trading partner to choose sides and raising the stakes for global energy markets while Hormuz stays closed.

sections.heading: Canada Walks Away From the Table as Trade War Escalates
sections.body:
The United States imposed 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian products early Saturday, and Canada said it would retaliate beginning 8 September after last-ditch negotiations collapsed, AP reports. Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended talks with President Trump rather than accept a deal he said the US 'asked too much' and 'offered too little' for, accusing Washington of a 'power play' with eleventh-hour changes.

Carney, one of the first world leaders to walk away from the negotiating table with the White House, told reporters 'you're at war when you're attacked — we got attacked.' Trump responded that Canada wants the 'benefits' of being a US state, per the BBC. Canada sends roughly 70 percent of its exports to the US, and states including Michigan, Kentucky, Indiana and Ohio are the most exposed to the fallout.
sections.whyItMatters: A decades-old free-trade relationship between the closest of allies now has no clear off-ramp, and Carney's gamble that Canadians will accept economic pain to stand up to Washington is being watched closely by other governments facing Trump's pressure tactics.

sections.heading: Ukraine's Political Crisis Deepens as Sacked Minister Demands Wartime Elections
sections.body:
Ukraine's dismissed defence minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, told the BBC that President Volodymyr Zelensky should be asked what he knew about corruption in his inner circle, pointing to a money-laundering investigation announced last week, while insisting he never saw the president act corruptly. Fedorov, who modernised the military and pioneered drone warfare, repeated his call for wartime elections, arguing 'democracy should not be the hostage of Putin.'

Zelensky rejected the idea, saying elections during a war would be 'a tsunami for the country that will split Ukraine.' The rift comes as leaders from the Nordic and Baltic nations gathered in Kyiv on Sunday for a summit on National Flag Day, pledging continued military and financial support, according to AP.
sections.whyItMatters: A public challenge to Zelensky's wartime leadership from a popular former minister, over both corruption and the suspension of elections, tests the political cohesion of a country fighting for its survival and could reshape Western assumptions about Ukraine's stability.

sections.heading: DR Congo and M23 Agree a Roadmap for Peace Talks
sections.body:
The Democratic Republic of Congo's government and the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group agreed a roadmap for peace talks after five days of negotiations in Switzerland, the BBC reports. In a joint statement they pledged to 'pursue negotiations towards comprehensive peace and conflict resolution' and set up a mechanism to monitor the ceasefire, with the first verification mission due Monday in Minembwe, South Kivu.

Disagreements remain over sanctions against M23, the release of detainees and the timing of political reforms. The talks were attended by M23, the DRC government, Qatar, the US, Togo, the African Union Commission and host Switzerland, building on the US-brokered Doha Framework Agreement signed in 2025. Fighting has continued in North and South Kivu despite repeated ceasefire commitments, in a conflict that has killed thousands and displaced hundreds of thousands in a region rich in coltan vital to global electronics.
sections.whyItMatters: A concrete, internationally backed roadmap with a ceasefire-monitoring mechanism is the most tangible step yet toward ending one of Africa's deadliest conflicts, with implications for regional stability and the global supply of critical minerals.

sections.heading: Coordinated Arson Wave Hits Thailand's Insurgency-Hit South
sections.body:
More than 50 coordinated arson and incendiary attacks 'aimed at creating unrest' were carried out across Thailand's southern border provinces between 20:00 and midnight on Saturday, the Thai military's Internal Security Operations Command said, per the BBC. Targets included a local government office, a convenience store, a stolen vehicle and telecommunication towers, with at least two people injured and an overnight curfew imposed in Narathiwat province.

No group claimed responsibility. The attacks come ahead of a two-day visit by Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and his cabinet to Hat Yai next week, and follow the killing of five soldiers at a Narathiwat checkpoint in July that postponed a planned peace dialogue. The low-level insurgency in the Muslim-majority south, led mainly by the Barisan Revolusi Nasional, has killed more than 7,000 people since 2004.
sections.whyItMatters: A coordinated, nationwide-style escalation in Thailand's long-running southern insurgency, timed around a cabinet visit, signals a breakdown in the stalled Malaysia-facilitated peace process and a renewed security challenge for Bangkok.

sections.heading: China's Property Fallout Reaches a Landmark Verdict
sections.body:
The founder of collapsed property giant Evergrande was sentenced to life in prison, the BBC reports, marking a key moment in the fallout from a collapse that shook China's property sector and rippled through the global economy. Separately, three Hong Kong activists were convicted in a national security trial for inciting others to subvert state power under the China-introduced law.

The verdicts come as Beijing hosts the second edition of its World Humanoid Robot Games, part of a broader push to project technological leadership, while the fast-fashion retailer Shein aims for a valuation of almost $27 billion in a Hong Kong stock market debut due on 1 September.
sections.whyItMatters: The Evergrande sentencing closes a chapter on the crisis that exposed the fragility of China's property-led growth model, while the Hong Kong convictions underscore Beijing's continued tightening of political control — both signals of how the world's second-largest economy is managing its internal strains.

bottomLine: The defining shift today is Washington's decision to wage economic war on Iran — a coordinated isolation campaign aimed at collapsing the regime, with details due at a press conference on 24 August and Tehran warning that supporting it would be an 'act of war.' That escalation, alongside Canada's decision to walk away from trade talks with the US, points to a world where economic coercion has become the primary instrument of great-power pressure. Meanwhile, a credible peace roadmap emerged for eastern DR Congo, Ukraine's political crisis deepened over wartime elections, and Thailand's southern insurgency flared in a coordinated arson wave. The common thread: the tools of statecraft are shifting from the battlefield to the balance sheet, and every ally is being forced to pick a side.
